title: The Hard Part of Dementia Care Isn't the Dementia—It's the Caregivers Who Get Dragged Down
dek: The difficulty of dementia care lies not in the patients' condition itself, but in the caregivers who are worn down day after day—care turns wives into nurses and forces post-90s to quit their jobs; love is a starting point but not a support, and the system hasn't caught up with these families.
why: This isn't a health science primer for the elderly; it's a sociologist's honest fieldwork inside dementia families: no standard answers, only realities you need to see before it's too late.
who: Only children born in the 1980s and 1990s, and urbanites whose parents are aging while they haven't made any eldercare arrangements; also those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care resource gap ultimately falls back on every family
points.body: China has 323 million people aged 60 and above, 23% of the total population; there are 35 million disabled elderly, but only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap isn't absorbed by the market or institutions; the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China accounts for nearly 30% of global cases, and the host estimates that on average, one in every 20 Chinese families is affected—for the first generation of only children, this may be the reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies are unreliable
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, Tang Yong most wants to correct the misconception that dementia patients have a uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia mostly comes from movies, neighbors, or hearsay; the incontinence of the professor in Still Alice is just one type. He met an elderly man who, despite dementia from his tailor background, would still notice stains on visitors' clothes and teach them to remove them with orange peel; he also saw an elderly woman who, after losing function due to a car accident, could only hum Liuyang River with focused expression. Dementia encompasses various causes like Alzheimer's and vascular dementia; each person's life imprint remains in different ways, and care cannot follow a script.

points.h: The dementia village ideal depends on national care insurance
points.body: Most people see the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: residents shop at supermarkets and go to cafes like normal residents, while staff pose as shopkeepers to maintain a normal atmosphere. But the host adds details that expose its low replicability—the 23 houses built in 2009 cost over €18 million, of which €17.8 million was covered by the government, and residents' costs are also covered by long-term care-related systems. In contrast, Tang Yong saw in a low-income U.S. nursing home that elevators must be locked to prevent dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease differs not in philosophy but in the national payment system.

points.h: Love isn't enough; sacrifice drags down caregivers
points.body: The host captures the caregiver's predicament well: many swing between "I love my parents very much" and "I'm about to be dragged down by them." Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse must learn to bathe, feed, and manage emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a beautifiable devotion: twenty years ago in Guangzhou, he interviewed a daughter who, after caring for her disabled father, divorced and fell into severe depression; the book also features a post-90s caregiver forced to quit their job due to care pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, caregivers also become patients.

points.h: The more you see, the less certain you are about eldercare
points.body: Having studied eldercare for years, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his own parents' care. He is a first-generation only child; his parents are both 75 this year, but the more cases he sees, the less certain he feels; his research assistant even says after each interview that the more families she sees, the less she knows how to arrange care for her own parents. Multi-child families also have friction: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough care causes bedsores; only-child families lack shared manpower, and some who moved their parents to Shenzhen find rent, medical costs, and nanny fees adding up faster than pension increases. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child independently.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that caregivers must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elderly man who could initially paint blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later only dared to praise others, afraid to put brush to paper; another elderly woman's husband reported new losses weekly: his wife couldn't recognize their daughter's newborn grandson, not knowing where this child came from. This daily, irreversible downward slide drains caregivers more than physical disability. The long duration of care is not repetitive hardship but facing a small farewell every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived but doesn't cover all elderly
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, and by around 2025 it will cover about 90 cities; the official pace is to move toward universal coverage in the next two to three years. But Tang Yong reminds that long-term care insurance doesn't give money to every elderly person; through unified assessment, it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home care, meal delivery, and other services; those with mild conditions may not qualify. The hardest part is also cultural: sending parents to a nursing home is often equated with filial impiety in China, and elderly people, like the grandfather in the interview, feel their hair will fall out within a month. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the proportion choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap won't disappear automatically.

So I think care should still be a kind of relationship. In this relationship, I think both the caregiver and the care recipient undergo great changes in identity, emotions, and even the pace of life.
It's like going down a slide—you're on a downward path. So at this point, I think this kind of care is indeed long.
I think although love is a very important foundation, it shouldn't be the only condition for care. It still requires some external resources, including social support, and so on.

Although the more I see and the more cases I encounter, it doesn't mean I have a very complete or perfect plan for my parents' future care. Precisely because I've seen so many different stories, it actually leaves me with more confusion.
